title: Judges 3:12–31
context: This passage tells of Ehud, the left-handed Benjamite whom the LORD raised up against Eglon king of Moab, and closes with a single verse on Shamgar. The account is vivid and detailed: the hidden two-edged sword, the private audience, the death of Eglon in his upper room, the delay of his servants, Ehud’s escape, and the rout of Moab at the fords of the Jordan, followed by eighty years of rest. The narrator tells the story plainly and without moral commentary, which leaves the reader to weigh Ehud’s deception and the violence of the deliverance within the wider frame of the book, where the LORD acts through flawed and surprising human instruments. Both traditions read the passage soberly: God is sovereign over oppressor and deliverer alike, he answers his people’s cry, and the narrative neither celebrates violence for its own sake nor holds up every method of a judge as a pattern for imitation. The notes avoid both caricature and comedy.

verses.text: The children of Israel again did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done that which was evil in the LORD’s sight.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel again does evil, and the LORD strengthens Eglon king of Moab against them because of that evil. The verse repeats the evil twice, framing Moab’s rise as the consequence of Israel’s unfaithfulness.

Arminian readers see God responding to Israel’s renewed sin with renewed discipline. The strengthening of Eglon is presented as a just consequence of covenant breach, aimed at bringing a straying people back rather than at their destruction.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the striking statement that the LORD strengthened Eglon; God’s sovereignty extends even over the power of a foreign oppressor, who serves God’s purposes without knowing it.

Both traditions agree that the verse places Israel’s suffering within God’s just rule, and that Eglon’s strength is not a sign of Moab’s gods prevailing but of the LORD disciplining his own people.

verses.text: He gathered the children of Ammon and Amalek to himself; and he went and struck Israel, and they possessed the city of palm trees.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eglon gathers Ammon and Amalek, strikes Israel, and takes possession of the city of palm trees, very likely Jericho, which is called by that name elsewhere (Deuteronomy 34:3). The coalition shows the scale of the threat.

Arminian readers note the sad irony that the first city Israel took by faith in the land is now held by an enemy. What was received as a gift can be lost through unfaithfulness, a theme the book presses repeatedly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the loss of the city of palm trees reverses one of Israel’s great early victories, showing how far the people have fallen from the days of Joshua. The LORD who gave the city now permits it to be taken.

Both traditions agree that Israel’s possession of the land was tied to covenant faithfulness and that this setback is part of God’s discipline rather than a failure of his power.

verses.text: The children of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel serves Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years, a longer oppression than under Cushan Rishathaim. The length of the bondage underlines the seriousness of Israel’s situation.

Arminian readers see the long servitude as a time in which Israel experiences the bitter fruit of its choices. God allows the consequences to run their course, giving the people space to recognize their need and turn back to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Israel serves a foreign king because it would not serve the LORD; the bondage mirrors the idolatry that caused it. God’s discipline fits the sin.

Both traditions agree that the eighteen years are not meaningless suffering but part of a covenant pattern in which oppression exposes Israel’s need and prepares the way for the cry and the deliverance that follow.

verses.text: But when the children of Israel cried to the LORD, the LORD raised up a savior for them: Ehud the son of Gera, the Benjamite, a left-handed man. The children of Israel sent tribute by him to Eglon the king of Moab.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel cries to the LORD, and he raises up Ehud the son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, who is sent with Israel’s tribute to Eglon. The detail of his left hand prepares for what follows.

Arminian readers note again that the LORD answers the cry of his people. Ehud’s left-handedness, which may have seemed a minor detail, becomes part of how God works through an unexpected individual whom he calls and sends.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers emphasize that the LORD raised up Ehud as savior, so the deliverance originates with God. The name Benjamite can be heard as son of the right hand, and some readers find a deliberate irony in a left-handed man from that tribe, though the text does not comment on it.

Both traditions agree that God often chooses unlikely instruments, and that the tribute mission becomes the occasion for deliverance.

verses.text: Ehud made himself a sword which had two edges, a cubit in length; and he wore it under his clothing on his right thigh.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud makes a two-edged sword about a cubit long and straps it under his clothing on his right thigh, where a weapon would not usually be expected. The narrator records his careful preparation without comment.

Arminian readers note that Ehud acts with real planning and initiative. The text does not portray him as a passive instrument; he takes responsibility for the task and prepares deliberately, and God works through that preparation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the narrator gives no explicit divine instruction about the sword or the plan, so readers should be careful not to treat every detail of Ehud’s method as divinely commanded, even though God raised him up as deliverer.

Both traditions agree that the verse simply sets up the narrative, and that the concealment of the weapon foreshadows a deliverance accomplished by a hidden blow rather than open battle.

verses.text: He offered the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud presents the tribute to Eglon king of Moab, and the narrator notes that Eglon was a very fat man. The detail is reported plainly and matters for the account of his death that follows.

Arminian readers note that the scene of tribute shows Israel’s humiliation under Moab. Israel is paying for the privilege of living under a foreign ruler, the outward sign of the bondage that its unfaithfulness had brought upon it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the description of Eglon is narrative detail rather than mockery. Some interpreters see in his size a picture of a ruler grown heavy on Israel’s tribute, though the text itself does not draw that conclusion, so the reading should be held lightly.

Both traditions agree that the verse should be read soberly, as a detail that explains what happens next, not as an invitation to ridicule.

verses.text: When Ehud had finished offering the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute.
verses.arminianNotes:
After the tribute is presented, Ehud sends away the people who had carried it. He separates himself from the others before carrying out his plan.

Arminian readers see Ehud acting deliberately to protect those who came with him and to carry the risk alone. The verse shows a leader who accepts personal responsibility for a dangerous task rather than exposing others to it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrative moves step by step, each detail preparing the outcome. The dismissal of the bearers is part of a sequence that the narrator presents as unfolding under God’s purpose to deliver Israel through Ehud.

Both traditions agree that the verse is a transitional detail in the story and that its significance lies in setting the stage for the private meeting that follows.

verses.text: But he himself turned back from the stone idols that were by Gilgal, and said, “I have a secret message for you, O king.” The king said, “Keep silence!” All who stood by him left him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud turns back at the stone idols near Gilgal and tells the king he has a secret message. Eglon commands silence, and his attendants leave. The stone idols may mark carved images or boundary stones; the exact sense is uncertain.

Arminian readers note that the deception begins here. Ehud says something technically true but intended to mislead, and the text records it plainly, inviting readers to weigh his method seriously rather than simply admire it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the narrator reports Ehud’s words without endorsing or condemning them. God raises up the deliverer, but Scripture does not thereby approve every means a judge uses, and the book increasingly shows the judges’ flaws.

Both traditions agree that the setting near Gilgal, a place tied to Israel’s entry into the land, may add weight to the scene, and that the deception is a real ethical issue for readers.

verses.text: Ehud came to him; and he was sitting by himself alone in the cool upper room. Ehud said, “I have a message from God to you.” He arose out of his seat.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud approaches Eglon, who sits alone in his cool upper room, and says he has a message from God for him. The king rises from his seat, perhaps out of respect for a divine word.

Arminian readers see a sobering moment: Eglon receives a message from God in the form of judgment. The oppressor who had been strengthened by the LORD now meets the same LORD’s verdict on his rule over Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the message from God is in fact the judgment Ehud carries. Whatever one makes of Ehud’s method, the narrative presents Eglon’s end as God’s act of justice against an oppressor of his people.

Both traditions agree that the verse is grave rather than comic, and that God’s sovereignty over rulers includes the power to bring their oppression to an end in his own time.

verses.text: Ehud put out his left hand, and took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his body.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud reaches with his left hand, takes the sword from his right thigh, and thrusts it into Eglon’s body. The detail of the left hand explains how the attack came unexpectedly.

Arminian readers note the human agency in the act. Ehud carries out the deed by his own decision and strength, and the text does not soften the violence, asking readers to recognize the cost and gravity of deliverance in a violent age.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the narrator records the killing in direct, unadorned terms. The act is presented as part of the LORD’s deliverance of Israel, but its violence should be read with soberness rather than celebration.

Both traditions agree that the verse belongs to a narrative of holy war in an ancient setting, and that it is described rather than prescribed as a pattern for believers to imitate.

verses.text: The handle also went in after the blade; and the fat closed on the blade, for he didn’t draw the sword out of his body; and it came out behind.
verses.arminianNotes:
The handle goes in after the blade, the fat closes over it, and Ehud leaves the sword in the body. The narrator’s detail is graphic and unflinching.

Arminian readers note that the narrative does not turn away from the reality of death. Scripture records this event honestly, and readers should neither linger on it for amusement nor pretend it was anything other than a violent killing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the detail explains why Ehud left without his weapon and why the servants did not immediately discover what had happened. The narrator is concerned with how the deliverance unfolded rather than with spectacle.

Both traditions agree that such vivid detail calls for sober reading, and that the passage shows the seriousness of God’s judgment on oppression without inviting crude humor.

verses.text: Then Ehud went out onto the porch, and shut the doors of the upper room on him, and locked them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud goes out onto the porch, shuts the doors of the upper room, and locks them. His escape depends on the locked doors delaying discovery.

Arminian readers note that Ehud’s careful action continues. He takes steps to secure his escape, showing that faith in God’s deliverance does not exclude prudent human planning and responsible effort in carrying out a dangerous task.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the narrative moving under God’s providence: each element, from the private audience to the locked doors, contributes to the outcome God intended, the deliverance of Israel from Moab.

Both traditions agree that the verse is a narrative hinge, and that the locked doors set up the delay that allows Ehud to escape and rally Israel. The precise layout of the room and porch is not entirely clear.

verses.text: After he had gone, his servants came and saw that the doors of the upper room were locked. They said, “Surely he is covering his feet in the upper room.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Eglon’s servants find the upper room locked and assume he is covering his feet, which is usually explained as relieving himself. They hesitate to intrude on his privacy.

Arminian readers note that the servants’ assumption gives Ehud the time he needs. The narrative shows how ordinary human expectations become part of the way events unfold, without any suggestion that the servants were acting other than freely.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s providence works through ordinary circumstances, including the servants’ assumption, to accomplish his purpose. The delay is not a miracle but a natural occurrence that God uses.

Both traditions agree that the euphemism is reported plainly and need not be read as a joke. Its function in the story is simply to explain why the servants waited.

verses.text: They waited until they were ashamed; and behold, he didn’t open the doors of the upper room. Therefore they took the key and opened them, and behold, their lord had fallen down dead on the floor.
verses.arminianNotes:
The servants wait until they are embarrassed, then use a key to open the doors and find their lord dead on the floor. The discovery comes only after a long delay.

Arminian readers see the end of an oppressor who had ruled Israel for eighteen years. The scene is sober: the power that had seemed secure collapses in a moment, and those who served him are left exposed and leaderless.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the LORD who strengthened Eglon has now brought him down. God raises up and puts down rulers according to his purposes, and the death of Eglon marks the turning point of Israel’s deliverance.

Both traditions agree that the verse should be read as a solemn reversal rather than a comic scene, and that its theological point is God’s judgment on oppression.

verses.text: Ehud escaped while they waited, passed beyond the stone idols, and escaped to Seirah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud escapes while the servants wait, passes beyond the stone idols, and reaches Seirah. The location of Seirah is not known with certainty.

Arminian readers note that the time Ehud gained by the locked doors becomes the time of his escape. His careful plan, carried out with courage, allows him to return safely and to lead Israel in the deliverance that follows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in the escape God’s preservation of the deliverer he raised up. The mention of the stone idols again frames the scene, possibly hinting at the contrast between those idols and the LORD who actually delivers.

Both traditions agree that the escape is a necessary step in the narrative, moving the story from Eglon’s death to Israel’s campaign against Moab.

verses.text: When he had come, he blew a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim; and the children of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he led them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud blows a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim, and the children of Israel come down with him as he leads them. The private act now becomes a public summons to the people.

Arminian readers note that the people must respond to the call. Ehud’s act opens the way, but Israel has to come down and follow, showing that God’s deliverance involves the willing participation of his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the trumpet as the signal of God’s deliverance being carried out. The LORD has already broken Moab’s power at its head, and the people now follow the deliverer God has raised up.

Both traditions agree that the leadership of the judge and the response of the people work together in this verse, and that the hill country of Ephraim becomes the rallying point.

verses.text: He said to them, “Follow me; for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand.” They followed him, and took the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites, and didn’t allow any man to pass over.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ehud calls Israel to follow him because the LORD has delivered the Moabites into their hand. They seize the fords of the Jordan and let no one cross.

Arminian readers highlight that Ehud gives the credit to the LORD and calls the people to act in faith on that promise. Their obedience in following and taking the fords is the faithful response to what God has declared he has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Ehud speaks of the deliverance as already accomplished by the LORD before the battle is fought. The victory is God’s work, and the people’s action is the outworking of what God has decreed.

Both traditions agree that this is the theological center of the account: whatever human means were involved, it is the LORD who has delivered Moab into Israel’s hand.

verses.text: They struck at that time about ten thousand men of Moab, every strong man and every man of valor. No man escaped.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel strikes about ten thousand men of Moab, strong and valiant men, and none escapes. The number marks the scale of the defeat.

Arminian readers note the seriousness of warfare in this ancient setting. The text records the totality of the defeat as the end of Moab’s oppression, while readers today must weigh such accounts within the whole movement of Scripture toward peace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the complete defeat as the LORD’s judgment on an oppressing power and his decisive answer to Israel’s cry. The strength of Moab’s warriors only underlines that the victory was the LORD’s.

Both traditions agree that the verse belongs to the ancient context of Israel’s wars in the land, and that it is a historical report rather than a model for how God’s people should act today.

verses.text: So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. Then the land had rest eighty years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moab is subdued under Israel’s hand that day, and the land has rest for eighty years, twice the rest under Othniel. The deliverance brings a long season of peace.

Arminian readers note that the rest is a gracious gift following Israel’s return to the LORD. It also gives the people an opportunity to remain faithful, which they will again fail to do when the next generation turns away.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the eighty years as a sign of God’s abundant mercy. Israel’s cry was brief, but the rest God gives is long, revealing a generosity that far exceeds what the people deserved.

Both traditions agree that the rest is the goal of the deliverance and that its eventual loss will show again the need for something more lasting than the rule of any one judge.

verses.text: After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who struck six hundred men of the Philistines with an ox goad. He also saved Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shamgar the son of Anath strikes six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and also saves Israel. His brief notice introduces the Philistines, who will become a major threat later in the book. He is mentioned again in Judges 5:6.

Arminian readers note that God uses even an ordinary farm tool in the hands of a willing man. Shamgar’s faithfulness with what he had becomes the means of deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the name Anath may recall a Canaanite deity, which some take to suggest Shamgar was not of fully Israelite background, though this is uncertain. Either way, the LORD uses whom he will to save his people.

Both traditions agree that the ox goad highlights a deliverance accomplished with humble means, showing that the power to save belongs to God rather than to weapons.
